summary:
Nicaragua does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or trans identity. The penal code that took effect in March 2008 repealed the 1992 sodomy provision, which had carried one to three years' imprisonment and whose vague wording had also been usable against LGBT-rights campaigning and sexual-health work.

Formal legality does not translate into protection. The US State Department's 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices in Nicaragua documents a police and parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived opponents of the government that authorities did not investigate or prosecute, and lists violence or threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex persons among the year's significant human rights violations. The official US assessment places anti-LGBTI abuse inside a broader climate of state impunity.

Amnesty International's May 2019 reporting on the crackdown that followed the April 2018 protests records at least 325 people killed and more than 2,000 injured, according to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights. The same reporting describes journalist Miguel Mora being beaten by a pro-government mob and states that he was targeted in part for being gay, an instance of homophobia operating inside the political repression rather than beside it.

For a visitor, the practical consequence is that no effective domestic recourse is visible in these sources: they document non-investigation and non-prosecution of state-linked violence, and Amnesty International describes a continuing government crackdown on independent media after the 2018 protests. Nothing in the source set identifies a functioning domestic complaint mechanism or civil-society channel through which a trans visitor harmed in Nicaragua could obtain redress.
tangentialFactors:
The defining feature of the risk picture is the gap between formal legality and enforcement. Conduct is not criminalised, yet the state-linked actors a visitor is most likely to encounter, police and pro-government paramilitaries, are the documented perpetrators of violence that goes unpunished.

Nicaragua's 2008 decriminalisation places it among jurisdictions where same-sex conduct is lawful while LGBT people remain exposed to attack. The operative variable here is state impunity rather than the text of the penal code.

Political and identity-based targeting overlap. The documented beating of a journalist targeted partly for being gay indicates that a visitor read as gender-nonconforming, or as an opponent of the government, may draw the same mob or police attention.

The scale of the 2018 crackdown, at least 325 killed and over 2,000 injured per the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, points to a general level of force available against civilians rather than a risk confined to LGBT people.
localsOnly:
Nicaraguan residents live under the same documented impunity. The US State Department reports that police and parapolice harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived regime enemies went uninvestigated and unprosecuted during 2023, with violence or threats against LGBTIQI people listed among the significant violations.

The 1992 sodomy provision's vague wording had been usable against domestic LGBT-rights campaigning and sexual-health work, so community organisations carried legal exposure even before the provision was repealed in 2008. The current source set shows the extra-legal pressure continuing in its place.

Independent media and civil society in Nicaragua have operated under a sustained government crackdown since the April 2018 protests, which narrows the organisations a resident could turn to after an attack.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Franklin & Marshall Global Barometers entry for Nicaragua records no documented finding for this jurisdiction, so survey-based evidence on public attitudes toward LGBT people remains unresolved here.

Recent trans-specific figures, including counts of trans women killed over the past two and a half years and NGO tallies of violence against LGBTIQ+ people in 2024, are not carried in the current source set and are unverified for this record.

The sources assembled do not address legal gender recognition or marker changes on Nicaraguan passports, entry or visa screening of trans travellers, restroom and facility access rules, restrictions on gender-affirming healthcare, hate-crime sentencing provisions, or recognition of same-sex partners. None of these can be stated either way from this inventory.
